questions.q: A hero wants to win a big court case but really needs to stop using people. What is Truby's name for the court case?
choices: Need
Desire
Ghost
Plan
questions.explain: Desire is the hero's goal in the world and drives the plot; need is the inner change.

questions.q: Why does Truby object to three-act structure?
choices: It has too many acts for television
It ignores page counts
It's mechanical: it imposes a shape from outside and says nothing about what should happen or why
It requires a conflict-free middle
questions.explain: Truby wants structure to grow organically from the hero's change, not be poured into a template.

questions.q: A writer's opponent is a generic villain who wants something unrelated to the hero's goal. What would Truby suggest?
choices: Make the opponent compete with the hero for the same goal
Cut the opponent and let the hero fight themselves
Give the opponent a save-the-cat scene
Move the opponent's entrance to page 12
questions.explain: Truby's best opponent wants the same thing as the hero and is best able to attack the hero's weakness.

choices: Four acts of roughly equal length
Four sequences in Act II
A hero, a main opponent and two secondary opponents, each in conflict with all the others
The four corners of the story circle
questions.explain: Each character stands for different values, so conflict runs in many directions at once.

questions.q: How should a story make its moral argument, according to Truby?
choices: Through a character who states the theme early on
Through the hero's actions and moral choices and their consequences
Through a closing voice-over
It shouldn't: stories are morally neutral
questions.explain: He warns against preaching; the argument is made through structure and should be felt, not heard.

questions.q: Which step comes immediately before the new equilibrium in Truby's seven?
choices: Battle
Plan
Opponent
Self-revelation
questions.explain: The order is weakness and need, desire, opponent, plan, battle, self-revelation, new equilibrium.

questions.q: Truby advises creating characters as a web rather than one at a time. Why?
choices: Because each character is defined by how they contrast with the others, especially the hero
Because ensemble casts sell better
Because every character must have the same arc
Because minor characters should be cut
questions.explain: Contrast sharpens everyone, and minor characters become variations on the hero's moral problem.

ideas: A story should grow organically from its premise rather than being poured into a mechanical three-act mold.
The best opponent competes with the hero for the same goal and is best able to attack the hero's weakness.
Build the cast as a web: four-corner opposition puts a hero and three opponents in conflict with each other.
A story's moral argument should be made through the hero's actions and choices, never preached.
